utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, 25th of November, 2008. Good morning to the four accused present today; two are ill. Good morning to the Defence counsel. Good morning, Mr. Stringer. Good morning, Ms. West, and good morning to your team and all the people assisting us. Mr. Registrar, you have an IC number for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prlic Defence has issued its objections to Prosecution exhibits tendered through Witness Tomic, Neven. This list shall be given Exhibit number IC 00894. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to read out an oral ruling which is rather lengthy, but, first of all, I'll ask Mr. Registrar to give us the number again, because it's not been recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said the Prlic Defence objections to Prosecution exhibits tendered through Witness Tomic, Neven, shall be given Exhibit number IC 00894. IC 00894.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've got it now; that's correct. The position of the Trial Chamber regarding the scope of the temporal jurisdiction of the second amended indictment. At the hearing of the 4th of November, 2008, Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Karnavas raised an issue regarding the interpretation of the temporal scope of the second amended indictment, and requested a hearing to be held that would be devoted to the issue. Such request, which was not expressed in a very precise manner, was made during cross-examination of Witness Neven Tomic by the Prosecutor with regard to facts about the period following the Washington Agreement. The Trial Chamber understands that the application by Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Karnavas deals both with the temporal jurisdiction of the second amended indictment and the admissibility of evidence related to facts following the period covered by the second amended indictment. With regard to the scope, the temporal scope of the second amended indictment, the Trial Chamber recalls that the relevant part of paragraph 15 of the second amended indictment reads as follows, I quote: "Between the 18th of November, 1991, or before that date, and April 1994, approximately or thereafter, various individuals set up a joint criminal enterprise and took part in it in order to subject, politically and militarily, Bosnian Muslims and other non-Croats living in areas of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were claimed as being part of the Croatian Community Future Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and to expel them, to ethnically cleanse the area or areas, and to gather within a short or long term these areas within a Greater Croatia or to join these areas as part of a Greater Croatia, whether in the short term or over time, and whether as part of the Republic of Croatia or in close association with it, by force, fear, or threat of force, persecution, imprisonment and detention, forcible transfer and deportation, appropriation and destruction of property, and other means which constituted or involved the commission of crimes which are punishable under Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Tribunal Statute." The Trial Chamber understands that the period covered by the second amended indictment starts on the 18th of November, 1991, and goes until April 1994, and that the accused are indicted for crimes alleged in the second amended indictment, alleged to have been committed during that period. Therefore, the second amended indictment does not, in the view of the Trial Chamber, hold accused responsible for crimes that would have been committed before or after that period of time. With respect to the admissibility of evidence on facts that would have occurred before or after that period of time, if such evidence is relevant, has probative value, and meet the requirements for admissibility of documents, as set forth by the Trial Chamber's decision in this respect, the Trial Chamber may admit such documents if they aim at proving the evidence that do not relate to a punishable behaviour by the accused, but to a general requirement for their responsibility, including the existence of a joint criminal enterprise which, in and of itself, would not be a crime. For the above reasons, the Trial Chamber considers that it is not necessary to hold a hearing devoted to such issues. This is the Trial Chamber's decision as to the temporal jurisdiction of the second amended indictment. I invite you to read it again later on, because it was a lengthy oral decision which is very clear for the Judges of the Trial Chamber. Let's have the witness brought in for the cross-examination to continue. I believe Mr. Praljak is ready. He's going to start. Mr. Kovacic, Mr. Praljak is going to take the floor, since we are dealing with military-related issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Mr. President. I would just like to remind the Court that according to the unanimous decision of the Chamber before the Appeals Chamber rendered its decision extending the right of the accused to cross-examine, that even at that time the Trial Chamber had decided unanimously that Mr. Praljak is qualified to examine the expert witness of the Prosecution, Dr. Ewa Tabeau. Since this expert testimony is directly linked to that evidence, I don't think that I have to repeat the arguments that were presented before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. General Praljak is going to cross-examine you. He may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, as you can see from where I sit, I am an accused in this trial. But for the purposes of you and your examination, I am a professor of Sociology. I have a degree in Sociology, so I feel that I am able and qualified enough to go through some of the issues that you addressed yesterday in your testimony. I would kindly ask you, as I guide you through this process, not to use scientific terms, such as creating a group, matching keys, and so on, before I ask you to do so. I would like us to go through those tiny elements first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, Your Honours, I ask you to interrupt me if at any point you want to ask any questions to clarify issues. Of course, this should not be deducted from my time. The year is 1991, and now I have to apologise to Mr. Karnavas for repeating and going through some areas that he's already dealt with in his examination. But at any rate, I hope you'll excuse me for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1991, there was this census. You made a plan, decisions were made, the methodology was put in place, and then some people got together and you trained them. They are the census-takers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And since the census is to be taken in a relatively short period of time, and there is a lot of stuff to take census of, there are many of those census-takers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The census-takers are human beings. As they go from household to household, errors are made in asking questions, perhaps suggestions are made, and the job is not done as it should be done. As a scientific, do you assume or do you know that even at that stage, we already have a certain number of errors and incorrect data?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a rather complex question. All the instructors training the people that will be doing the census try to train the census-takers or interviewers how to do the proper methodology. They receive instructions that they have to comply with. So even if they are unable to memorise the instructions, they receive those instructions in written form as an aid memoir. In the course of the interview, an instructor monitors the interviewer, by primarily checking whether any systemic errors are made; for instance, if a question is asked in a different way, is misinterpreted, or is skipped. But it is a fact there may be an influence of the interviewer to a smaller or greater extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if I may, I would just like to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, if I had three or four hours to deal with this issue, I think it would be enough for us to deal with everything quite specifically, but my time is very limited and I have some major issues that I need to deal with. So let us address those. We know that errors are there, corrections, samples that are then controlled -- undergo additional controls, but I'm sure you're familiar with that. Let us move on. When those papers are all put together in the same place, it's in the Institute of Statistics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, they will.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, they go to the municipal commissions, the census commissions, and then they are sent to the Institute of Statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let us see what is being recorded and why. We want to know the first and the last name of a person, male or female. Then we want to know how many men we have, how many women. We want to know the ethnic affiliation, which is voluntary. You can decide what you want to put in there. Then we want to know the age, children up until the age of three, five, and how many elderly people. We want to know how -- the number of livestock, sheep, cows. We want to know how much of the housing is privately owned and how much is socially owned. We want to know how many refrigerators we have in the state. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. Statistics do not want to know the first and last name. It's not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. So, for instance, if we have a census in France and we say that we will have an increase in the number of old people, then if we determine that, then the president says, "Well, who is going to feed all those old people? We don't have enough young people. So let us increase the pensionable age"; would that be so?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then we see the qualification of those people, how many people graduated from high school, university, and so on; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now we come to the important point. All these data will be separated from the first and the last name?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's important. All the data, the acreage of land, the number of refrigerators, these are all sets of data, separate sets of data; and once they're processed, they have nothing to do with the first and the last name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Those papers that come to Sarajevo, they are put into an optical scanner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, yes, that is correct. Before that, it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: We speak about 1991. So the optical scanner, it scans, let's say, Croats and then enters the value "1." I'm simplifying things. I'm trying to simplify things so that they're extremely clear. Yugoslav Croat 1, Croat 1, yet another Croat. In the end, we will get the total of Yugoslav, of Timbuktuan?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify this. All the questions that are asked in the form are given a numerical form. The interviewer asks the question about the national affiliation. He has to put down the word "Croat, Serb, Muslim, Turk," and so on. Before statistical data are processed, they have to be encoded. There are code books and nomenclatures which clearly state, if it's a Croat, you have to write down "1"; if it's a Serb, you have to write down "2"; if it's a Montenegrin, you have to write down "3"; if it's an Englishman, "9"; if it's a Frenchman, "10"; Yugoslav, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That's the point I was driving at. First of all, the interviewers write in their own hand, and their handwriting may differ. And as far as I know, there can be errors there, because it may be misread; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to give you an example. In 1991, the optical scanner, not only in Bosnia but in many republics, turned out to be quite impractical, because it requires you to write down a figure very clearly. I was in charge of the 1991 census, and it happened to us, after the optical scanning was done, that we had a village of Velika Drenova, and we had all the population of Velika Drenova turned out to be English people speaking Danish as their mother tongue. It's a small village. The problem was that the optical scanner could not read the figure correctly: "9" was interpreted as 0, "6" was interpreted as 0. I wrote a paper which was published about the problems encountered in the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear from you. So at that time, when you could see that the optical scanner caused mistakes, then you will get a sample of, let's say, 100 forms; and then you process them manually to see how many mistakes this optical scanner did?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How did you do it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the processing, when you enter some data into the optical scanner, and it turns out that they are wrong, you have to consult the original source, the form, and check the suspicious data. That's the first level of verification. People who are entering data at the first stage do that. After that, you have a number of other checks, logical and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please slow down and not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, what I want to know is this: Let's say we have the municipality of "A," and Judge Trechsel, His Honour Judge Trechsel, goes there and he meets Praljak. We sit down and have a little chat, drink some wine, and His Honour Judge Trechsel wants to know my ethnic background. If he is allowed, and statistical processing is not done because of the tax, the internal revenue system, or for the purposes of the intelligence services, he cannot go to the database and learn from the database whether I was a Croat, a Muslim, or what; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He cannot get any individual data ... [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So this is very important. We separated those sets, and we know, for that locality, that there is a certain number of Croats, Bosniaks, Serbs, Yugoslavs, and that a certain percentage of housing is privately owned, social owned, and so on and so forth. But we do not know -- we cannot establish a link between the first name and the last name and all the other data; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: This brings that point to an end. Let's move on. This was 1991, and now we come to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In light of what General Praljak just said and your answer, I would like to refer to the encoding process. In my understanding of what you said, ma'am, the forms are filled out by those people who are asked questions in the census, and then the person is charged of encoding, in other words, given a figure. For instance, if it's Muslim ethnicity, then a given figure will be given. So I wonder, I have questions about those who actually performed the encoding. Could there be political belongings of these people and, therefore, they would tend to say there are more Muslims than Croats? You have been involved. I would like to know whether these people who are performing the encoding were actually controlled, in a way, or supervised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about encoding; not decoding, but encoding. There are special code books for every area; ethnic background, profession, the line of work, education, gender, marital status, and so on and so forth. All this is expressed in figures, and the figures are in code books. Encoding is done by professionals. This is a major task, and, again, there is a competition for temporary employment. People who are selected are educated, literate, capable of performing a task. They are provided with a set of instructions, and they have a controller. I personally believe that whoever has done that job was good, and it has nothing to do with politics. It is not just one person who encodes the one village. We're talking about census regions which can be part of a settlement. For instance, Mostar can be divided into several regions, and when you put them together, you end up with the whole picture. I believe when it comes to people who encode data, there is such a possibility, but there has never been any abuse. However, this has never been investigated, and it's very hard for me to claim with any certainty that there, indeed, has not been abuse at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Professor, now we come to the war. Let's not go into the genesis of the conflict, because this is not what we're here for. All sorts of things happened to people. They move, they leave their place of residence, they're expelled, they're ethnically cleansed. Whether they are refugees or displaced persons is a legal issue, not a demographic issue; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. And if you look at the instruction for the registration of voters, OSC provides its explanation, which says displaced persons are all the persons who have voluntarily or forcibly moved out of their place of origin. The legal definition is something else. The statistics don't have its definition. But if we were to embark on a research, we would rely on the legal definition thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's an entirely different story. In 1997 or 1998, OSC says to Bosnia-Herzegovina and its state organs, "You will not have nothing to do with the elections, it will be our job"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You don't know. Very well. Let's move on, then. However, at that moment in 1997 and 1998, according to you and the data known to you, how many people of all ethnic affiliations had changed their place of residence? How many went to Germany, Hungary, Finland, Norway, Croatia, Serbia, and so on and so forth? According to you and the data available to you, was that figure over two million?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read different authors, originating from different states of the former Yugoslavia. The figures differ, but it's always in the millions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It has been noted as anything between two million upwards. OSC says, "Now you have to vote. Register to vote." You can register from any place of residence where you reside now. You can vote anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly, but there is such a possibility. OSC, according to the instruction that I am aware of, says the following: All citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina over the age of 18 can register to vote. They have to be on the 1991 census. However, a precedent is made here and it is said, if you're not on the 1991 census, you can still prove that you're citizens. If you don't have a single document to prove you're citizenship, you can, in the presence of a judge, in the presence of a religious leader, in the presence of two witnesses who will testify on your behalf and are registered in the census, and they can all say that you are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And based on that, you will be given the right to vote because you are, indeed, a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Let's assume that all of us sitting in this room were residents of the Municipality A; and for various reasons that are explained by Lee, by the law, sociology, and politology, we moved out. For example, His Honour Judge Trechsel lives in [indiscernible] and deals with [indiscernible] equation; His Honour Judge Antonetti is admiring Rodin's sculptures in Paris; at the same time, His Honour Judge Prandler is drinking Tokaj on Balaton Lake. They all used to be citizens of that municipality; and from the representative offices of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the respective states, they get forms to register for votes?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they're citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: They all say, "We will vote in the Municipality A that we're talking about." Wouldn't that be the situation?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a recommendation for them to vote in the municipality where they resided in 1991, but there is again a precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it says, due to the number of displaced persons, irrespective of the motives for which they were dispelled, it is also possible for them to vote in their current place of residence if you can prove that you arrived before April 1996. I can't give you the exact date. You can even vote in a municipality where you want to vote, if you reside abroad, if you have valid prove why you want to vote there. In other words, there are precedents, and you can vote even in your future place of residence or your future municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I understand that, but let's talk about the most important point, which is the following: There's voluntarism involved there. Everybody has the right to vote of their free will?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And after that, when we come up with the sum of those who voted, it is an arbitrary sum?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the census, yes, that will be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, with respect to the census. That depends on people's way of thinking. Some will say, "I've had enough of the state, of the war, of politics, and I don't want to vote"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this very day, in peace time, you have people who don't want to come to vote; they don't want to come to the polling station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to the data available to you at the recent elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina which took place a couple of months ago, of anything between 800.000 and a million people residing outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina and are still residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina, only 30.000 registered for local elections?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to talk about figures, but, yes, the figure is low. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, the figure is low. Now we have ended up with a sum which is very important for us to be able to see what is the turnout of voters, but we don't know what else to do with that, in terms of scientific approach?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, that will be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's go on and move a step forward. Ms. Tabeau says, "I don't have any money. There was no money at the time for a new census. We can't go to the same municipality and do the exercise all over again. There's no money." Then she says the following, "I'm going to take this sum that I have received, and I'll try and see what had happened there in migration terms." She says as following, "First of all, we have to say, from the people who registered, who is of what ethnic background, because they don't have to declare that when they vote. They don't have to say, 'I am going to register as a Croat'"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speeding because of the damn time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then on the list in Municipality A, she finds the name "Karnavas," and she doesn't know what to do with that family name, whether that person is an American, a Greek, or something else. Then she refers to the database in the census, but there she can only check whether "Karnavas" was registered in that municipality. Again, she can't find his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she can, because in a census, in what Bosnia and Herzegovina has at the time, there are names. Dr. Tabeau will find the material of the entire census of Bosnia-Herzegovina by names. First, there is name, then data for the municipality, for the census district, males, females, and so on and so forth. Whether the name is transcribed accurately or not is a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you saying that she has papers rather than sets?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dr. Tabeau will have that in electronic form. In an electronic form, she will have the entire census of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and she will have individual data. Everything has been scanned, so the first datum is name. If you photocopy once in the list, it will start with a name which is composed differently. First of all, you will have "Svetlana Radovanovic, gender," but it will start with the municipality and the electoral district. Everybody who is -- who knows what they're talking about will know what figures stand for. So she will end up with computer codes where she will be able to find the name. But the number of mistakes in the names was absolutely incredible and beyond belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's take, for example, if you want to learn Petkovic's ethnic background through their name, how many Petkovics are there in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I know how many Kovacevics there are in Croatia because it was recently on a pop quiz.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Croatian and Serbian family names are very frequent and they're very common, and it is almost impossible to determine the ethnic background of a person sharing a certain family name?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: For example, Slobodan Praljak, if we are trying to assess the situation, Slobodan Praljak would be a Serb sooner than a Croat; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the methodology you want to use, then, yes, I would be tempted to say "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. So, in this way, the lady in question arrived at a certain number of data on the people who voluntarily voted. That figure is not big. It has to be augmented. Did she join to that number the person's family members?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and it does not say anything about that in the report. I can only tell you what I think. In the case that we are discussing, and we are discussing the census compared to the electoral rolls, she does not have joint family members if she is certain about the name. But Dr. Tabeau says something else in her report -- or, rather, her testimony that I listened to. She says, "When I'm not certain -- when I wasn't certain about a name, a family name or a personal name, I used the household method." That method is absolutely nonexistent in statistics, but it exists in the computer code. Members of a household are added to a certain name. "Household" is an economic category which can be complex. It can be a family or it does not have to be a family. "Household" can be composed of people who are related, but it doesn't have to be. Living in a household does not mean that everybody has to share the same family name. In the former Yugoslavia, several generations would very often share one household. For example, you had parents living with their married daughter, son-in-law, and grandchildren; and, automatically, you have two family names. For example, I could be living with my son-in-law and my daughter. We would still be one household with two different family names, because my son-in-law, my daughter, and my grandchildren would bear a different family name than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And Mrs. Tabeau, for the lack of any better elements, used something that you called a "key," and she added that to the basic person; and then she would say this is a Croat, a Serb, or a Muslim, without going into the issue of mixed marriages and so forth. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. When you say "key," this is the way how you can match things. My key would be the name, the family name, and so on and so forth. This key, the name, the family name and the year of birth, is something that I migrate into the census, and I look for the matches. Whatever is matched, I can then say, "Yes, now I have a match between Svetlana Radovanovic, on the one hand, but I have three Svetlana Radovanovics in the census." Under the assumption that her name is in the electoral roll, Dr. Tabeau will end up with three Svetlana Radovanovics of different ages, and then she will say, "I have this as a match, I will take her, and I will discard the other two." Maybe she can say it can be any of the three. But I think the fact that you're not absolutely certain must have an effect on the number of matched cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And we will be finished with this topic soon. Let us assume that we have Municipality A and that in Municipality A there live a certain number of Croats and Serbs, but there are no Muslims. There used to be Muslims, but there are no Muslims anymore.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1997. In the census, you had a certain number of Serbs, Croats and Muslims; and now, for some reason, Muslims left, and Serbs and Croats remain there in a certain proportion. But for some reason, Croats and Serbs say, "We don't want to get involved in politics. We don't want to register to vote. There are no parties that we want to vote for. We don't care ," and Muslims, who are no longer living there, register to vote. What would we get then? According to Ms. Tabeau, what kind of a set would we have?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all those people who did not register, you could not get a match.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked to not overlap because it is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if you don't have people who registered, then you cannot match them. But if they are in one set, you will find them in the other set, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I asked you a quite specific question. So those two groups, Croats and Serbs, did not register to vote. Will this result in a fact that with the application of Ms. Tabeau's method, there will be no Croats in that place because they did not register to vote?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's what I wanted you to say, but now we can have the whole situation --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, please, let me just -- I apologise. I did not give you an accurate answer. There will be Croats as they existed in 1991, but there will be no Croats as recorded in 1997. So you could see that there were a certain number of Croats in that place in 1991, according to the census; but if they did not register to vote, they do not exist on the voters' lists. If they do not exist in the voters' list, you cannot find them in the census in order to be able to say, well, this is a Croat, so you cannot achieve a match. Then in 1997, you will say, "I did not find, or I found three, or I found five." So they cannot appear there unless they are registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, that's what I wanted you to say. So it's possible, it's a possible scenario, creating such sets can lead to stuff situation, where in reality we have only Croats living in that area, or only Croats and Serbs; yet, because they did not register to vote, they disappear from Ewa Tabeau's tables; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For 1997, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we can make all kinds of permutations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I kept silent so far, but I have to say again, please, don't torture the translators. It is really very difficult to follow you. You speak, both of you, in your mother tongue, and that is why you have to take care to stop after a question and after an answer and then continue. Please be so kind to be kind the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are really trying. Please believe us when we say that. But it always ends up this way. I have to apologise both to the interpreters and to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So that's what I wanted to hear from you, this conclusion. By the application of this method that we now explained step by step, what Ewa Tabeau obtained in this way is a virtual world, a nonexistent world that may contain a number of errors and, therefore, may not have anything to do with the actual situation in the field in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, when His Honour Judge Antonetti, referring to the table yesterday, makes the calculation, and His Honour Judge Antonetti is very good with his sums, is it true that he is making a total of virtual figures and that they may correspond, but because of the application of this method, you indicated that the margin of error is up to 60 per cent in relation to the actual situation in the field in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really say "yes," because there's another element here. The figures that you're looking at, that Dr. Ewa Tabeau obtained, are figures where she says -- she says, "I claim that these are the persons," but we do not know how reliability the figures are. We know that the figures are not full because of all the people who did not register to vote. We know for sure that there were modifications in the application of the matching method. We don't know to what extent and what they were. We know that for this -- for the figures that she's showing there, that there must be some people that we can claim with some reliability that they really exist. But now as to what part and what proportion of people, we can say that they possibly existed, but there is a high degree of doubt. I cannot tell you that. This is what I was talking about yesterday, that the Prosecution expert provided the statistics of the matching process, and she said that, "This matching key is reliability and, that is how I managed to obtain a 50 per cent match. I have a high degree of acceptability -- I can claim with a high degree of acceptability that these are the same persons. And as for the rest, I used a different key. The probability that these people are one and the same people, that they're properly identified, is lower ." This is very important. So I cannot claim what is accurate and what is not accurate. What I can claim is that data are unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, this is what I wanted to ask you, but let us go a little bit deeper into that and we'll leave it at that. If you had a student and if you gave him this as an exercise, would you ask them, at any -- every step of the matching process, to calculate the margin of error; is that correct, would you do that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And in that manner --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they cannot calculate the margin of error.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, reliability.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The degree of reliability, in light of the matching key, is high.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I misspoke. The degree of reliability. But now you tell me -- or, rather, you told us yesterday that the degree of reliability of these data -- or, rather, the degree of unreliability was between 30 and 60 per cent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In light of the data sources that have the margin of error between 30 and 60 per cent, I cannot say that the reliability of data is greater than that. With reference to the data sources, I can say that the reliability is doubtful to that degree, at least. Let me underline, for statisticians and demographers, the non-existence of data, which is, in fact, then when you invent the data, it is an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If you create data in a scientifically unacceptable manner?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, with reference to something that Mr. Karnavas asked you, in every other aspect, did she apply the same or similar methodology?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific? What do you mean, "every other aspect"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What she says about the people killed, wounded. In other words, when she created the sets, did she apply the same unreliable methodology as she did here. So we don't know what area was covered, we have a smaller set, and the results are transferred to a larger set without any critical approach, as she did when it came to the killed and the wounded, as you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we cannot generalise. When it comes to the ethnic background and refugees, the area that Dr. Tabeau is analysing is quite clearly defined. It's the eight municipalities. So we know the area. But the methodology that she uses to determine the ethnic background and the number of refugees and displaced persons is completely wrong and scientifically unacceptable. You asked me to tell you whether it is the same. In the two analyses that she also conducted, we don't know the area. The area is not defined. There is East Mostar, but we don't know what that is, to the left of the Neretva River. Another thing that is quite interesting: The methodology used to determine the ethnic background is not the same. So Dr. Tabeau did not take the first name, the last name, and year of birth from the register and then compare it to the census and then determine ethnic background, but what she said is, "I'm going to take the first name and last name, and then I will take the frequency of the name." So we're not talking about matching. We're now talking about the frequency method. "I will determine the ethnic background." So if there are more Svetlanas among Serbs and Svetlana is a Serb, and if there are more Svetlanas among Croats and she is a Croat, so it is not a matching method, but frequency. But when it came to the war hospital books, the frequency method is not used by her, but she says, "I have experts assisting us to determine, on the basis of the first name and the last name, who these people are." So we are talking about two methods: The frequency method and experts who determine the ethnic background. So it's a new method, as opposed to the determination of the ethnic background on the basis of the census results.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is this scientifically acceptable anywhere in the world?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never encountered anything of the sort, but what I find more interesting here is why the same method that Dr. Ewa Tabeau claims is a good one, and that is matching, is not applied in both reports, because the same data exists in both cases; first name, last name, year of birth, year of death. So I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, among Muslims and Serbs, and even among Croats, is "Zoran" a very frequent name?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not really study the frequency of names, but I know Muslims, Croats and Serbs alike whose first name is "Zoran." I don't know the frequency of the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's say "Jasmin," "Jasmina," and so on and so forth. Can we consider this method to be unreliable to a high degree; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not scientific method at all; it's just a coffeehouse debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at 3D 03259.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really find my way around, because I don't have the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 3259. Somebody will assist you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 446. You have a table here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The author of this document is General Drekovic. It's a photocopy. General Drekovic became the commander of the 4th Corps after General Pasalic. In his book, he provides some tables, and I would just like us to look at them very briefly. So this is the information provided by General Drekovic, who in late 1993 became the commander of the 4th Corps, and that's the BH army corps that defended Mostar, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, madam, in this table - we will say that, well, Their Honours know that, but you don't know that - we see that there is the 6th Corps. The Judges know where it was and so on. But now I would like you to look at page 475. Have you been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, let us just look at those figures, and could you please memorise them? Mr. Drekovic says that in that corps, which in the previous -- but I will explain that later, probably, that by the 19th of January, 1994, so in 1993 and in the 19 days of the year 1994, 579 soldiers were killed in his corps, and that he had 1.168 wounded. We can simply say that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here. Now, if, for any reason whatsoever, but we will not do that because it is not proper, if we were to accept Ewa Tabeau's information about some 500 people who were killed in Mostar between May 1993 and April 1994, could we then say, "But these are all soldiers who were killed," because Drekovic says here that he had 579 men killed and 1.000 and so on wounded. 579, yes. So there's no civilians killed, it's all clean, there were more soldiers who got killed than were listed as killed in the war hospital books or in the register of births. So if we were to play her game, would we conclude that? I'm sorry, I'm sorry. So if we were to play this matching game, could we then say, "Well, Your Honours, Ewa Tabeau claims that there are 500 people who are dead, and Mr. Drekovic says, 'I have 579 dead soldiers,' so all the people who are dead are soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Praljak, I would not like to play this game. This is really guesswork, and I would not like to engage in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We will not engage in that, because we know for sure that civilians were killed, too. But then it should not be calculated using Ms. Ewa Tabeau's method, but you will agree with me that the forensic medical documents are the basis for the determination of who got killed or who died where, when, why?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree with you then, and I can challenge, from the scientific point of view, the figure that is given, the 539 people, but it has nothing to do with this document. I can draw your attention to the following thing: Dr. Tabeau, as you saw, does mention the cause of death in her report. In the register of deaths, no cause of death is recorded. There is another thing which is called a death certificate. A death certificate is a document that is issued by the coroner, and this death certificate is taken to the registry and it is kept there in permanence. But the information from the death certificate is not recorded in the register of deaths. Dr. Tabeau does not refer to the death certificates as her data source, but she takes the cause of death from the register of deaths. That's what she says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So, very quickly, you already spoke about the term "siege" that is used by Ms. Tabeau. Did you find anywhere that she defined what a siege was?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said yesterday. There is no definition of "siege."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Moreover, we're given a military map to depict the places where HVO units in Mostar, the BiH Army, and the units of VRS; did you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received some maps, I can't say they were military maps, and they depicted the division of Neretva into West and East Mostar, by the Neretva. I never asked for military maps. I never received military them. I probably wouldn't be able to use them. If Dr. Tabeau had used them herself, then I would certainly study any such maps very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, I would now kindly ask you to take -- I'm just looking for the number. I'm talking about her two reports. I'll probably have the time only for the first one, and the number is P09837. These are Ms. Tabeau's reports, firstly.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need assistance. I can't --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What report?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: About the people who were killed. And while you're looking for it, let me ask you this: The term "killed" and "fallen" in the Serbian, is it one and the same thing? Is it true that soldiers fall and killing is a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A fallen person does not have to refer to just a soldier. You can fall in a traffic accident. The causes of death are separate, and we're talking about violent deaths. For example, violent deaths may be due to an accident, a murder, and so on and so forth. So there is a very exact division, because all violent deaths do not imply only people who fall in the war. There are also people who were killed in accidents even during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In this part that speaks about the deaths in East Mostar, did you ever come across any suicides, that persons were killed in traffic accidents, that they were killed from mishandling of arms?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau did draw a table with 497 persons. I may not be correct, but if you allow me to refer to the material --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Be my guest, of course. This is table 16. In B/C/S, it is the 26th of 32 pages, table 6.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not talking about any tables. I'm talking about a list of the persons who were registered as dead in the death certificate or death registry and people who died in the war hospital. According to the military hospital book, 474; and according to the death registry, there were 400 and something. If you look at the lists, you will come across a number of persons who were killed in traffic accidents or other sorts of accidents, and I believe that there is one person who committed suicide, and I quote their names in my report. I'll try and find them and tell you exactly which persons I am referring to when I speak about these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, I apologise. I don't really have an interest in those people.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I just came across it. It says "Gemma, Handzo, born in 1959, was killed in a traffic accident near Tekija," and there are other such cases and persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please now open table number 3 for me on page 10. This is Ms. Tabeau's report about deaths in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, this is what Ms. Tabeau says here. The table is here; and for Mostar, we have "Unknown, 135," yes, "389," "524"; and then she says, and I quote: "The total number ..." -- This is an overview of valid cases for municipalities, and for relevance for the siege of East Mostar. Ms. Tabeau says that this is relevant for the siege of East Mostar. Then, further on at the bottom, she says this: "The total number for Mostar municipality is 524 records, see tables 3 and 4, out of which," pay attention, "out of which only 373 records fall under the strict requirement of being relevant to the siege of Mostar." In brackets: "I.E., death occurred in East Mostar during the period May 1993 to May 1994." Closed brackets. Ms. Radovanovic, if somebody says scientifically that this is the number that fall under the strict scientific criteria, how would you go about augmenting that number? The augmentation of that number, wouldn't that be a game of adding apples to pears to mice and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't go about augmenting the number. However, the explanation itself speaks about all sorts of combinations, speculations that went into the figure. That fact that it falls under the strict requirement of relevance, and you still don't know what the criteria are, but I believe this is based strictly on dates, i.e., on years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, please open the following page, and you will find table 4 on it, and everything is repeated there, and Ms. Tabeau also repeats here: The number of 373 records, recorded in East Mostar during the siege, is considered relevant and valid for the purposes of the analysis of the victims of the siege. Please, I would like to hear your comment.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any comment, sir. Again, how shall I put it? This is Dr. Tabeau's position, which is not based on the reliability of the data that she has. If you don't know, what area are you dealing with? If you don't know, I really can't comment upon this. This is another speculation, another statistical speculation on her part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's one problem. However, a second problem is this: When she established the figure of 373, without talking about soldiers or anybody else, and she says, about that figure, that it is relevant and valid, how would it occur to you to augment it, and what would you then do with that augmented figure?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau has two sources for reliable and valid data. One source is the book of births, and that's what she looks at; and the second one is the war hospital. Then she is combining and says, "This is what I'm going to take from the register. I'm going to add to that what I found at the war hospital. This is what I saw in the document called "Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and this is what I saw in the Croatian Army. Then I am going to put all that together and end up with 529." Now, when you look at all these tables that you have in front of you in the report, and when you then look at the table that -- table that gives you the grand total that refers to all victims, and their number is 539, then you will see all sorts of combinations that went into coming up with that figure. Just let me -- bear with me for a moment. I'm trying to find the table. I've marked it in my Serbian version -- or, rather, I did not. Please bear with me. I would like to show you what sources she used and how they contradict each other. Look at table 13, please. These are grand totals of Ms. Tabeau's findings. This is an overview of accepted records of the sources, when she looked at the death register, the war hospital. I'm not going into the method of how she segregated cases. She said that there are 539 cases of whom she identified 370 in the death registry, and I accepted this. To the 134 from the war hospital, I added the 370 because they were taken from the war hospital as accepted. However, in the documents of the army, in a document entitled "Dead Soldiers" or "Fallen Soldiers of the BiH Army," which comprises all soldiers from 1992 to 1995, I found 29, and they were not in any of my two previous sources. I found them, and based on the date, they died from April 1992, and I added them as well, and in the same source, I found the fallen soldiers. So that would be the grand total. All the tables in front and most of the story, with all due respect to Dr. Tabeau, are actually the analysis of the sources based on the method what would happen if that was the case, and the result is a product of a number of statistical speculations found in the previous tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Radovanovic, could you please look at table 5 for me. It says here, and I'm going to ask you something: "The number of deaths as a result of the siege, as recorded in the books of the Mostar war hospital." In your science, and particularly in sociology and sociological-psychology, there is something that is known under the name of correlation, putting two variables together. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: According to what you know, Ms. Radovanovic, the existence of correlation, can you automatically say that one is the cause of the other?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about science, but there's no science here. There's no correlation here. This is just an arithmetic exercise. She says, "I took this from here, that from there and I'm going to give you what the result of the math exercise is."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to assume even further. Even if we assume that we will accept Ms. Tabeau's numbers and figures, would it be admissible to write that this was the result of the siege? A siege would be a variable in this case. What would be the correlation between that variable and this, and can that first variable be proclaimed the cause without analysing every single thing that went into each death individually?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't know the cause, you can't proclaim any correlation, as such. If you don't know, that goes into that correlation. Maybe Dr. Tabeau knows, but she does not give us a definition. Maybe she should explain the correlation between the cases and the siege that she mentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And here, then, we would have to know - and we don't know - who was firing, from what side fire was opened, to what place, whether the fact that fire was opened, was it opened on a military or a civilian target. This should have been documented, photographed, and then we would come to the cause. Would that be a valid method; maybe very general, but this would be the cause for a possible correlation, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday, I spoke about the three methodological steps that Dr. Tabeau makes mistakes in. One is analysis, and the second is causal research. "Causal research" means establishing cause and consequences. If you don't know the cause, you can't explain consequences, or you can explain it any way you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, how much time do I still have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you have used one hour and six minutes, so you must have, at most, four minutes left, since you said yesterday that you needed one hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Then let me go back to the table that you, Ms. Radovanovic, looked at yesterday, and that's table -- I have it here. Just a moment, please bear with me. Table 16. We looked at it yesterday. Please, table 16. This is the one that I want to look at with you. It's the same document, table 16, page 26.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Again, in point four, Ms. Tabeau says the causes of death of the victims of siege, there is no doubt in her mind that these were the victims of the siege. But let's go on. It says in table 16, the distribution of the victims of the siege according to the cause of death, and yesterday you stated, Ms. Radovanovic, that 76 fell victim to shelling, 34 were killed in some way; gunshots, 18, wounding, 6; murder, 1. It seems that "killed" and "murdered" is not the same. When it says "murdered," that would be homicide, and "killed" would be just fallen in action or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In my view, murdered and killed are one and the same, but there are also instances of suicide. So I really don't know what Dr. Tabeau meant when she says "murdered."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And, now, when we added all that up, we ended up with 135 people altogether, and Ms. Tabeau says, and I quote: "It is clear that a large number of deaths were reported without mentioning any cause of death at all (404)." The doctors or whoever was there looking at those bodies did not mention anything. They were ignorant. In 404 cases, they didn't mention anything. But let's go on: "This doesn't mean that the unknown causes were unrelated to the siege." For God's sake, Ms. Radovanovic, my brain has stopped working when I was reading Ms. Tabeau's report. Can you understand what she's saying?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She's just speculating, Ms. Tabeau is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is beyond the pale. Those comments are not needed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you done, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Tabeau says, "I have a set of 135 units. That's not sufficient." Then she says, it is probable, it doesn't mean that it isn't. So if it means that it doesn't mean that it isn't, it means that it may be. Then she says, "On the basis of the assumption," "on the basis of the assumption," please read that closely, that unknown causes may have the same distribution as the well-established causes. A fuller estimate was made and presented in table 6. So could you please tell me, Ms. Radovanovic, what assumptions must exist in science in order for you to be able to go from a smaller set to the larger set, claiming that you are applying proper scientific methodology?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know what assumptions these are in scientific work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let me tell you. For instance, in physics, as a science, we can say that the space, the universe, is amorphous. We can say that if in an area we have a density which is such-and-such and it has been proven that the universe is amorphous in every direction, then this density that we managed to calculate as such in a smaller area, we can extrapolate that to every other area, assuming that the universe is amorphous. Can you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, although I'm not a physicist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: But do we have that here?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. This completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We're going to take a 20-minute break, after which Ms. Alaburic will have the floor for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to resume. I think that Mr. Stringer wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours and counsel. Just a very brief request. I'm being told that we have about 138 documentary exhibits that the various Defence teams are tendering into evidence through the previous witness, Mr. Tomic, in the various IC lists that have been filed, and one of which I think was the 1D -- or the Prlic team filed their IC list yesterday afternoon at the beginning of the court, which is what the Rule requires. But because of the number of documents involved and the quick turnaround time, we're asking to have a very short extension of time until tomorrow morning for the Prosecution to file its response to the Defence IC documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The Chamber has just deliberated and grants this request, if there are 138 documents that require some time for you to consider them, and, therefore, you are given time until tomorrow morning. Madam Alaburic, you have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honours, good morning. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me introduce myself. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I am an attorney from Zagreb, and in this trial, I defend General Milivoj Petkovic. You won't have many problems with me in my cross-examination, because, as you know, statistics was always the most difficult exam for most of the lawyers in the former Yugoslavia, so we're not that good with figures. My questions will be fairly simple, and I hope that you will be able to help me clarify some details. First of all, I would like to ask you this: I would like to ask you about causes of death, as information that is listed in the protocols of the war hospital. Let me remind you that Prosecution expert indicated that according to the data from the war hospital, for 44.4 of the cases, the cause of death was unknown. That's 209 out of a total of 472 persons. The Prosecution expert concluded that unknown cause of death from the war hospital mostly pertained to persons who were killed, persons who were killed. And on the basis of this claim in the expert witness's report, His Honour Judge Antonetti asked her what led her to conclude that unknown cause of death could be considered as death caused by -- that those people were actually killed, that this was the cause of death. Prosecution expert Tabeau said that the war hospital was not a regular hospital which treated persons who had other conditions, that this was a war hospital treating only victims or casualties of war. After that, His Honour Antonetti asked about the treatment of civilians, because from an earlier testimony, we were aware of a pregnant woman who, on the 9th of May, 1993, was taken to hospital. Ewa Tabeau answered, "For most of the deaths, the cause is not listed, but we had reason to believe that those were victims of the siege." I quoted this from pages 21.879 of the transcript -- 21.872, I apologise, and 21.873. Now, Ms. Radovanovic, as you analyse the expert report produced by Ewa Tabeau, listed -- all the causes of death listed in the protocols of the war hospital in East Mostar were as violent deaths?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She, in fact, stresses that, highlights that in her report. She says these were all violent deaths and that they were caused by war, a result of the war; although, as I tried to show from some examples, in the examples and the list of persons that Ms. Tabeau put together that I obtained from the Demographic Unit, you can find some cases that have nothing to do with that: A traffic accident or a suicide. I did list some of those examples in my report. So I don't know what reason justified Dr. Tabeau to consider all the causes of death as she did, because nowhere in her report does she say why she does it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let me now tell you what Dr. Rajko said in his evidence. During the war, he worked as a doctor in the war hospital in East Mostar. He said that in the war hospital, all surgical cases were taken in, regardless of whether those were hernias or inflammation of the bowels. That's recorded as page 12.911 of the transcript. It is also important to note what he said about the records kept in the war hospital. He said that up until the 15th of June, 1993, there was a single -- single records were kept for all the patients, peacetime and wartime, as they were called. And on day, a new recording system was set up, separating the records of those who were casualties of war; whereas, in the old records, continued to record the so-called peacetime cases. This is recorded at transcript page 12.934. Now, Professor Radovanovic, on the basis of this evidence given by a doctor who actually worked on -- in the hospital, would an expert of your kind conclude that the records of the war hospital also include records of the peacetime and wartime cases alike; or would there be a basis to reach some other kind of conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the scientists knew that, knew about this statement, then they would know that these deaths were of a different kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it then be justified to conclude that had Expert Tabeau had this information about the contents of the protocol of the war hospital, would it be difficult to imagine that she would disregard the data about the peacetime cases and would treat all the cases as violent causes -- caused by violence?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what other sources she used from other sides, because Dr. Tabeau does not indicate that in her report, but she notes that she considered only the cases from the war hospital that were the result of the siege. So I assume that she may have been able to look at all those materials, or had she been able, that her opinion would be different. But that's just my opinion. I don't know what Dr. Tabeau actually did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you some questions about the distribution of the unknown causes of death, proportionate to the number of known causes. You testified about that, and I think that you explained that in such a way that it was crystal clear. But in this context, I would like to draw your attention to this: In Ewa Tabeau's report, and that's document P9837 - you can see it in the Prlic Defence binder - in paragraph 23, registers of death are mentioned. It is noted here that out of 1.387 cases, the cause of death is known -- out of 1.383 cases, 132 cases are known. Let me correct the number -- yes, it's okay now. So for 1.383 cases, 132 cases the cause was known. Out of that, 89 deaths were violent deaths, and 37 natural causes. So if we look at those absolute figures and turn them into percentages, it turns out that about 28 per cent of the known causes were actually natural causes of death. Professor Radovanovic, could you tell us whether the percentage, the 28 per cent, is something that would be statistically relevant as a value?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In relation to 100?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really be very specific here, because we're talking about 1.383 cases that are taken out of 10 registers of deaths from certain areas. In those cases -- or in those registers, you have cases recording people who died in Vienna, but who were recorded in the registers where they had permanent residence. Now, whether 28 per cent of the 10 registers is relevant, I really can't tell you with any reliability, because you have to look at the overall picture, at the whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. But before I do that, let me ask you this question: As we continue -- or as Ewa Tabeau continued analysing the causes of death, she decided to take all the deaths that were caused by natural causes, whether the result of accidents or suicide, to rule them out, to exclude them from her data, and she disregarded them. She disregarded at least 28 per cent of known causes of death as something that might be relevant for her further analysis. Those were so-called natural causes of death. And in this manner, by eliminating natural causes of death, she increased the percentage of violent deaths in cases where cause of death was known; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau believes that there were no natural deaths during the siege of Mostar, and she only dealt with violent causes. That, of course, is not a comprehensive approach, and it is not professionally proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe you wanted to make the same point, Ms. Alaburic. But I see in the paragraph 2.3 on page 5, English version of the Tabeau report, that she speaks of the natural causes, "(37)," are the second largest. So, obviously, she was aware of the fact that they were natural causes. Ms. Alaburic has as the subject of her question the fact that she then puts those aside, but she has not ignored them. She just didn't take them into account. What is the effect of that, I think that was your question, if I interpret you correctly, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me to ask just one more question, it will become clear why the elimination of natural causes of death is important to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it is not controversial that Ewa Tabeau was aware of the natural causes of death. We see that she eliminated them from her analysis and that she focused only on violent deaths; and, thereby, the percentage of the ratios of the violent deaths, in fact, was increased, because natural deaths were eliminated. Now let us look at what happened when 404 cases, where the cause of death is unknown, are distributed proportionately to all the known unknown.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor Radovanovic, could you please tell us, among the criteria for distribution, do we have natural causes of death in, let's say, about 30 per cent of the cases? And if we had that, would the distribution of the unknown causes be different, given the situation -- or, rather, if we compare it to the situation where we have eliminated natural causes?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have to give you a more comprehensive answer, because I think there is some confusion here. Dr. Tabeau states, on the basis of the ten registers of deaths, that there are violent and natural causes. Then she says, "But out of that set that encompasses natural and violent deaths, I will not be dealing with violent deaths," and violent deaths thus becomes the set that becomes 100 per cent. This is not a comprehensive approach, because you could give the overall death rate and then you could say such-and-such percentage is the natural death and the rest is violent death. But an expert can do that. It's perhaps not entirely proper, but it can be done. So she says, "I will deal only with violent causes." Table 16 shows you this distribution for violent deaths, but I don't know what criteria were applied to distribute all the unknown -- or, rather, to classify all the unknown causes as violent deaths. She assumes this, that given the nature of the times, they had to be violent deaths. So out of a total number of deaths, she takes out only the violent deaths and establishes a different set, but the quantity is smaller, the numerical basis smaller. And on the basis of this numerical base, you get a different set of percentages. So if you were to calculate or to add the 135 or 137, whatever it is, to those numbers, you would not have 539 or 639. Then you would say, out of those 600 and whatever, 50 per cent are unknown causes, 10 per cent is natural causes, shelling is 3 per cent. So by dividing up this set and by classifying unknown causes as violent deaths, we get a different set of assumptions for a group, a different group that Dr. Tabeau declares to be a group of violent deaths. Why does she say so? She doesn't say that, but I would like to stress that she has the right to create a separate group that she wants to study; although, I think it would be proper to present the figures for the overall mortality on the basis of the register of deaths and the mortality that she ascribes to violent causes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, I think there is a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have been overlapping. You started asking the question long before the translation was done, so perhaps you start again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, I wanted to correct the error of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Page 44, lines 13 and 14, Professor Radovanovic, it was recorded that you said: "I will not deal with violent deaths," and I think that your sentence was actually: "I will deal only with violent deaths." Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What you have just told us at great length, I believe everybody understands, and it is an answer to my question, and an answer that I actually expected.
