But if we were to put things in very simple terms, then we would say that in table 16, there was also a category of natural death; then the total number of deaths would be higher, but the distribution of unknown would be different, i.e., there would be a lower percentage of those that were killed by shelling, because you would have entered a different variable for distribution?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the distributions would be different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I wanted to emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Ms. Radovanovic, you doubt the assumption of the expert, Tabeau, that unknown deaths there means deaths as a result of violence. Do you take into account, when concluding this, that originally she had 37 cases of what she calls natural deaths, which I presume are illnesses, sepsis in operations, and so forth. So is it not sort of natural to conclude that as these have been eliminated already, that the others are violent or, in other words, non-natural deaths, letting aside from the moment the cause, of course, which can be, as you rightly say, accident, suicide, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would like to draw your attention to the figure 37. Expert Tabeau deals with very precise data. According to her, 89 persons suffered violent deaths. So she knows the causes of death for 132 persons. This is in paragraph 2.3 of her expert report. The causes of death are known for 132 cases. She says violent death, 89, which is 67 per cent; and she says natural death, 37, which is 28 per cent. I believe that we cannot assume that from 37 to the total number of 1.330 dead, we can apply a valid conclusion that their death was violent. I would like to correct the figure on the page that we have on the screen. The figure is 1.383. The data that we are aware of is 37 and 89.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer His Honour Judge Trechsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An unknown cause of death, as the name has it, means that nobody knows the cause of death. If you don't know the cause of death, you don't know whether it's a natural or violent death. There are two possibilities here for something to be expressed as an unknown cause of death. The first would be totally unknown information, no diagnosis or anything. The second would be something that is done in the demographic statistics. For example, you can suffer from a disease, but your cause of death may be a totally different thing, a totally different illness. I, for example, God forbid, may be taken to hospital for cancer; however, in the course of that same night, I may die of a heart attack. In my death certificate, the cause of death would be "heart attack." The underlying cause, something that helped the cause, is a different story. That's why death certificates are issued by the physician, coroner. Then he's the one who has to investigate what illnesses the patient suffered from, how much influence that had on the death, and, finally, enters the cause of death. If physician, in normal situations, and I believe that in the war he may not be 100 per cent sure because somebody may have been wounded, somebody may have undergone a surgical procedure which failed, if he's not absolutely certain what the cause of death is, then the most common entry would be "Unknown." In the category of unknown causes of death, you cannot assume that all the deaths in there are violent. There may be other reasons why the cause of death is unknown. These deaths may be the consequence of different situations. For example, there may be the condemnation of the wound due to the poor conditions in the hospital. So the cause of death of a wounded person does not have to be the wound itself. If the wound becomes septic, then the cause of death would be a sepsis, not the wound. Since the expert worked on the basis of the war hospital book, I wouldn't be able to tell you who was it who entered the causes of death in the war hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm aware of all that, of course. The question is probably one of terminology. I would have put most of what you have now mentioned, in particular the heart attack, under the heading of "Natural causes," and we have no bases, really, to know what the criteria were. So would you agree that this is, all in all, it is rather in the vague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, particularly the war hospitals and their books and their registers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, you have tried to explain to everybody here in the courtroom that Ewa Tabeau's expert report is not an analysis but, rather, a presentation of her own databases and her own conclusion, if I understand you properly. You're saying that this is not an analysis because her report does not provide any comparisons with anything else, so that, for example, the information on 539 victims does not mean much if we don't know the share of the population that that was at the moment in East Mostar. Did I understand properly your general assessment of the expert's work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I answered it properly. But I would like to underline that Dr. Tabeau does not call her second expert report the statistical or demographic analysis of mortality due to the siege of Mostar. She calls it an analysis of death registries and books of the war hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to the second analysis that you've just mentioned, Expert Tabeau, in her conclusions, states that among the victims of the siege, and we will not dwell upon the term of "siege" at the moment, there were 49.5 civilians and 50.5 soldiers. We're talking about percentages here. We all know how Ewa Tabeau established the status of the military. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that during the hearing of Ms. Tabeau, His Honour Judge Antonetti put a very important question to Ms. Tabeau. The question was whether analysis had been made of all the available data according to the criteria of the age structure of the male population, in light of the fact that it is a generally-known fact that the regulations on defence in the former Yugoslavia and in all states of the former Yugoslavia prescribed that men of military age, between 16 and 65 years of age, have certain obligations in the defence of the population, and that a huge number of those who left the country had been of military age. The data is on the men of military age and their obligation towards the defence of the country and the doctrine of the General People's Defence, are you aware with all of that as a citizen of the former Yugoslavia, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data that may be drawn from the census can tell you how many men are of military age. You can then talk about military doctrine and say whether they are fall under the obligation of serving in the army. But what you don't have is where East Mostar is, how many live there, how many men, how old were they. So you don't have those types of analysis. If you don't have the specific territory, then you have a problem, because this does not lend itself to analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Despite all these shortcomings and disadvantages in the analysis of Expert Tabeau, I propose that we take her data on 539 victims and that we also accept her data on the gender and age structure of the victims, which is given in table 18. Then I would kindly ask you to analyse the documents that have already been admitted in evidence and to try and come up with a simulation of the share of victims in the population of the same gender, same age, and to see how this would reflect in proportions when it comes to victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to be using the document in my set of documents which is under seal. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I don't know if we have to go into private session or we will simply not transmit the document in e-court. Very well. It won't be transmitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be quick, Ms. Alaburic, because you've already used up your time. We're not going to broadcast this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would kindly allow you to -- I would kindly ask you to allow me to do this simulation and deduct any time that is the surplus from the overall time of General Petkovic's case. You will find the document as the last in my binder without any number, because it is not going to be in evidence. I would kindly ask the usher to put the simulation on the ELMO for everybody's benefit in the courtroom. The document that I said was under seal --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to object. I understand that this document was under seal, and I'm wondering if it may be more advantageous to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that before you render your decision, I'm going to use just one page of that document, which is page 7. Just a moment, please. It's page 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, just say that on page 7 of the document that you're not going to disclose the origin of, we have some statistical figure, and then you can put your question. Furthermore, the Registry is not going to display this document outside the courtroom, so it's not going to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit P09851. The page in B/C/S is number 7; and in English, it is ERN number, in the upper right-hand side corner, 137344. I'm going to be using only that one table. We also have another document which is 4D 01277. This is the population of BiH according to the census from 1971, 1981, and 1991, sorted by age and gender. We're going to be using the data from those censuses, and I would like to repeat the number of the document in the English. I correct the 4D number. It is 4D 1277. All the relevant data are in the document that has just been put on the ELMO for us. It arises from the document on -- it's page 7 with the aforementioned ERN number. Actually, this is a list of neighbourhoods in the municipality of Mostar. For the purpose of our analysis, I'm going to exclude neighbourhoods under numbers 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 because these are not in East Mostar, in the narrow sense of the word. I'm going to be dealing only with the data that we receive if we total the figures of neighbourhoods from 1 to 7. If we look at the figures, we will see that there were 10.161 locals and 17.066 refugees, or a total of 27.277. The figure of 55.000 refers to the entire municipality of Mostar. As far as the refugees are concerned, I'm going to be using a claim from the same document, in paragraph 2.10, where it says that those were mostly the families of detainees or smaller groups of detainees who had been released from prisons. Those were all elderly persons and infirm, in a poor physical condition. Based on that claim, I shall consider that the data, about 17.066 refugees, is the data that concerns women, children, and people above the age of 65. In document 4D 1277, you can see the breakdown of the BH population segregated by gender and age, and the total population of 4.373.033. The men -- I'm repeating the number, 4.377.033. The share of men of the military age between ages of 15 and 64 is 1.500.373, which account for 34 per cent. If that percentage of 34 per cent is applied to the data on the local population of East Mostar, i.e., if we're looking for 34 per cent of 10.161, we will see that in East Mostar there were 3.455 men of military age, and that the remainder of the local population, together with the displaced persons, accounted for 23.772 inhabitants. If these absolute figures are converted into percentages, it arises that the number of -- or, rather, the percentage of men of military age was 12.69 per cent, and that the remainder of the population accounted for 87.31 per cent of the total population. If such a population structure is then correlated with the victims, there are a total of 539 of those, according to Expert Tabeau. Among the victims, men of military age would total 37 -- 375, and others accounted for 164. 375 would be men of military age, and others would be 164. If we try to establish the share of victims in the population of the same kind, i.e., the share of victims among male of military age, in the population of males of military age, it arises that 10.85 per cent of that same population were victims, and that in the remainder of the population, 0.69 per cent were victims. If we now correlate the percentages in their relative relationship, it arises that men of military age did get killed during the siege of Mostar, or the so-called siege of Mostar, five times more often than -- 15 times more often than the other population.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ms. Radovanovic, I hope that you've been able to follow me. I tried to simplify things. Based on all the data that I've just presented to illustrate the significance of analysis and establishing of ratio, wouldn't this be a fair representation, a mathematical representation, and whether such a mathematical representation would be relevant for an analysis that Ms. Tabeau should have taken and, at the end of the day, for your analysis as well?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Calculating shares within the general population is always relevant; but, with all due respect, I have to say that this calculation, according to -- that you did this calculation in accordance with the method used by Ms. Ewa Tabeau. This is the distribution method. You say East Mostar had such-and-such a number, and so on; and then we assume if the overall population of Bosnia had this structure, then we can apply that to East Mostar, too. The method you applied, in other words, is not reliable. You can do this kind of calculation. This is a figure that might point you to something, but I personally would never engage in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I may just tell you right at the start, that is why, right at the beginning, I said that I wanted to show this to you to illustrate the point. I'm perfectly aware of the fact that it would be the same method. I'm perfectly aware of the fact that the distribution of the male population in East Mostar at that time may have been completely different. But I told you that on the basis of the information from one document that is already admitted into evidence in this trial, we tried to illustrate the relevance of such information. So it's simply to illustrate, not to prove that my calculation is right. Would you consider that this is a statistically relevant indicator?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an illustration or as an example, it is significant to see what real statistical and demographic indicators have to offer to those who know about statistics and those who don't, because it gives us a qualitative evaluation of a situation in a given moment, in a given population.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This was precisely what I wanted to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hold it for a minute, because there's a question I want to ask you. On the top of this paper, top left, we have the number "P09851," which suggests that this is part of a document that was admitted. In fact, Ms. Alaburic, I got the impression, and please tell me whether I'm right or wrong, that the expert who established these figures is Ms. Alaburic, is that right, or your Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you look at the upper part, you will see that this is information from document P9851, if you look at page 7 in the B/C/S version. That's the ERN number that I've given you in the English version. The second segment of this document that is on the ELMO now is the information about the displaced persons, and the conclusion about who those displaced persons are is based on the statement in paragraph 2.10 of the very same document, P9851. Your Honour Judge Trechsel, this is, of course, something that I did on the basis of the information that is known, because I thought that I had to illustrate to you that the conclusion of Ewa Tabeau that soldiers and civilians were killed in similar -- that they had the similar shares in the overall number of those killed, 49.5 were civilians and 50.5 per cent for the soldiers, because it is statistically insignificant because it warps the situation as it was in East Mostar. I think this is an indication enough that this is where we have to look at the truth about the victims in East Mostar. We should follow this path.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is what I had assumed, and I thought it would be good to have it clearly in the record. You took figures actually from what is called Attachment 4 of the document with a number, and then all the calculations you made on the basis of a selection of the relevant quarters of Mostar that you selected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the relevant parts of Mostar, I don't think that there is any doubt about where Blagaj is and that Blagaj is not in East Mostar. I thought everybody in this courtroom knew that and that there was no need for us to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will be 15 minutes taken out of your overall time, because you've used 15 extra minutes for your cross-examination. It is now on the record. What do we do? Do we have a break now or you can start? Whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. We're ready to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My name is Kimberley West, and I'm a lawyer with the OTP. In front of you, is that your report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... have available the OTP report as well?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Here on the floor, and it will be brought up to you, are three binders, and there are documents inside that I will refer you to. You'll note on top that there are little red tabs. Those tabs are actually on the B/C/S pages.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I think, Professor, it may be easiest if you just keep your report close by. Thank you. Professor, I noted on your CV that in less than 20 years, you've published over 20 scientific reports, and that includes your ICTY reports. In this list of selected works, have you published more than is noted on your CV?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list is not exhaustive. It does not include only reports concerning the court appearances. These are papers published in scientific journals. So the papers that are listed here are not reports that I did for court. There is a paper that deals with Srebrenica, but it was published in a compendium of papers of the School of Geography, which is considered a scientific publication.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. You just indicated that the works on your CV are the ones that are published in journals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I assume you're familiar with the concept of peer review.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. No work can be published in any scientific journal, at least where I live, unless it has been reviewed and unless the review was positive. Then it's published.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And one of the important notions of peer review is to ensure that the work is objective, it's unbiased; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every reviewer, undertaking any kind of review for the purposes of the publication of a paper in a journal, definitely risks his own or their own authority and will not allow the publication of anything that is not proper and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you say "proper and accurate," would you also agree with me that it would also have to be objective and unbiased?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every scientific works should be objective and unbiased, because science strives for reaching objective truth. Of course, I do not claim that each and every paper is objective and unbiased, but that is the desire, and that is why we have reviewers to assess that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I assume you, yourself, have been a reviewer.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Have any of the works listed on your CV been the subject of international peer review ?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not subject of international peer review, because all the journals that I listed are published in Serbia, in journals that are significant -- scientifically significant at national level. So they did not undergo international peer review, but they were reviewed by relevant scholars in the area where I live. I would just like to note this: It is not an author who appoints the reviewers. There is a number of scientific papers. The procedure goes as follows: I write a paper and I offer it for publication to a journal, and then the journal appoints the reviewers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, then, you would agree with me that you've never published in an international journal, you've only published in Serbian journals?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only in Serbian, but could you please define "international"? Does it include the army of the former Yugoslavia or globally?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Globally, a journal that is published outside the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did work for the European Centre and the Centre for Peace at the United Nations. These were huge studies. I really don't know, I didn't ask about it, but I do believe it was published internationally, because the president of that body was --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on. I assume, Professor, that you're familiar with the concept of complex humanitarian emergencies.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please define it? Could you please define whether I'm familiar with the concept of complex humanitarian emergencies?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Look to your left and grab binder number 2, and please turn to P10729. The B/C/S is the red tab on top. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think you have to go one more page. There you go. I'm going to read an excerpt from this exhibit, and then you can give me an answer with regard to whether you're familiar with this concept. This is from "Force the Migration and Mortality," and it reads: "The term 'complex humanitarian emergency' is widely used to described ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have the page, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll start again. It's page 1 of the English, and page 1 of the B/C/S: "The term 'complex humanitarian emergency' is widely used to describe a particular type of disaster: A situation in which a large civilian population ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't follow because it doesn't say that in Serbian. Perhaps I have the wrong document in front of me. Is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor Radovanovic, if you can actually listen to the interpretation, that might be the easiest way.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the interpreter is interpreting this differently, and the different word that is used gives a completely different sense. So if I listen to the interpreter and if I read the translation, these are completely different things. If I'm looking at the right document, it says "complex humanitarian dangers." But, please, I mean, we have to agree in order for me to be able to follow. Can I read what it says, and then we will agree whether this is proper or not; or perhaps you can give me a translation that contains the same -- that is conceptually the same. If I look at the right document --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out loud in English. It's going to be interpreted in your ear. Listen to that interpretation. If, afterwards, you want to dispute the actual interpretation, you can to that on redirect. I'm now going to read it in English, and you can listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not a matter of disputing. It's not a matter of disputing. First of all, I only have one page. I don't have the whole document. I'm not making a stink. My colleague should know better. I'm entitled to the whole document, not just one page. That's number 1. Number 2, they've taken the time, I assume, to translate it. One of the reasons is so the witness can read it. Now, apparently, she's getting two different versions. She's being asked to give an opinion, and now she's being cornered to one version versus the other. Now, she can pick or choose; but in my opinion, the witness has indicated she would like to read the version that was translated for her. She can read it, at least, and then she can hear whatever the translated version is. But I think we have to be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karnavas has a good point. If she can just read the B/C/S translation, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The best would be for her to read the text in her language loudly, and then the interpreters will translate. This way, we can check the English translation; and if there is a dispute, we'll realise right away. All right. Madam Radovanovic, can you please read the first paragraph loudly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The term 'complex humanitarian dangers' is often used to describe certain kinds of large-scale accidents, a situation where a large portion of the population is at risk from a combination of a civil or international war, or efforts to rearrange the state or society, such as, for instance, genocide, which lead to mass movements of the population, with the concomitant deterioration of the conditions of life; for instance, food, water that can be carried with oneself, shelter and sanitation, creating conditions for a substantial increase in the mortality normally through a limited time period, but sometimes over longer time periods." I have a footnote saying that this definition was taken from Tool and Waldman, 1997. It has been changed to a certain degree in order to be able to encompass several kinds of complex humanitarian organisations. The text goes on to say: "People always created complex humanitarian dangers. A simple and arbitrary example of this would be the attack of the Romans on Carthage, the attack of the Goths on Rome, and the conquest by the Islamic and Crusaders forces. The complex humanitarian dangers in the 20th century includes the Holocaust in the 1930s and 1940s in Europe, the famine in Bengal in 1943, the murders and the expulsion of the Chinese from Indonesia in the 1960s. The examples of complex humanitarian dangers over the past few years are wars, ethnic cleansings forced migrations, and genocide that occurred in wildly different areas, such as, for instance, Somalia, Bosnia, Rwanda, Kosovo, Sierra Leone, and East Timor."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, my question to you is whether this is a concept in which you're familiar.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether I'm familiar with the concept that is expounded by Messrs. Tool and Waldman which was later expanded, no, I'm not. This is the first I've heard about it. Now, if you ask me if I know what humanitarian crises are, then I do know that, and what humanitarian danger is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to go back to the Galic testimony in which you testified here in the Galic case in March 17, 2003, and you were read the same extract. When asked whether you were aware of it, you indicated on page 21.390, line 17, that you were currently involved in a project in Serbia addressing the same subject. You went on to say that you had heard about it. So my question to you, Professor, is whether this is a concept with which you're familiar and upon which you have worked.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the problem is that I wanted to read it, instead of having it read to me. It is possible that the Prosecutor may have read out the concept to me and asked me if I was familiar with it, if I knew what it was, but I don't recall having said that I worked in accordance with this concept. But I did work in many situations that could be considered as humanitarian dangers or emergencies. So what you are quoting for me from Delic -- from Galic, somebody read it out to me and I agreed that I was familiar with it. You have transcripts here. I don't know whether anyone named the authors of the concept; although, if I can remember, there was a name that was given of an author that has nothing to do --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours and my learned friend, I think that we could perhaps solve a problem here. To me, the term "complex humanitarian danger" is quite unfamiliar. I tried to find this term in our languages on the internet. This term does not exist. We use the term "crisis," and this is the term that Professor Radovanovic used. Perhaps we have this communication background because we use a different term than what the literal translation of the term "emergency" might be. So if we could ask the witness about humanitarian crises and projects that relate to that, perhaps then we could get the proper answer. I do apologise for standing up, but I think that this was a useful intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, would you consider the war in the former Yugoslavia as a scenario that fits within the parameters of complex humanitarian crisis or danger, however you may want to call it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you want to take me away from the area of demography, but I do think that every war, every large-scale event that can affect the population could be considered that; a tsunami, war, storms, earthquakes. It's just a question of scale.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question is very exact in this matter: Would you consider the war in the former Yugoslavia to be considered a complex humanitarian crisis?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to tell me, what is a complex humanitarian crisis? If you think that a complex humanitarian crisis is what is given here as a definition, then I would tell you yes. But everything is complex. You have a war zone where the situation is very complex, and areas where it is less complex. But if you want to generalise, it is a crisis, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me, again, direct your attention to your Galic testimony. On page 21.392, you were asked whether, in that case, whether you would consider the circumstances between 1992 and 1994 in Sarajevo to be a situation of a complex humanitarian emergency, and there you said, "Yes, you could put it that way." So bearing that in mind, again I'll ask you one more time: Would you consider the situation in Western Herzegovina to also be a complex humanitarian crisis?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please define the whole of Western Herzegovina. I'm sure that parts of Western Herzegovina did have -- did face complex humanitarian crises, just as Sarajevo did. But there were parts of Western Herzegovina where the crisis existed, but it was not as complex. You cannot generalise things; or, rather, I do not accept this kind of generalisation, because these are very serious matters and they are very complex. So if you give me the specific localities --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Fair enough. The eight municipalities that were the subject of the OTP report, those municipalities, do you consider that to be a complex humanitarian crisis?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what period, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In the period it was studied. So in the period, specifically in Mostar, let's talk about 1993.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not study that, because there's no data from the demographic point of view. I could not study it from the demographic point of view, and I did not deal with history, or politics, or any other such thing. There are no sources -- no demographic sources which would lend themselves to such a study.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I'm going to turn now to your Popovic report -- the Beara report, and that's P10724. That's in the first binder, the other binder.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would be grateful if figures, numbers, and quotations could be read out more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. It's 10724. It's at page 10 of the English, and page 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Binder 01724, you're saying, and page?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 9, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you? It's the red tab.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Now I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, so, this is the report you wrote in the Beara case; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose. I can't see the whole report. I can see just page 9, so I suppose that that has been my report taken by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't have the English version, one provided to the Defence. I don't know if the Judges have the English version, but I surely would like to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read out the second paragraph and then I'm going to ask a question. In this, you wrote: "The fact is, however, that in abnormal situations like war, there is usually no verified official statistical data for particular time periods and occurrences; and, thus, some international organisations recommend the use of data sources which do not satisfy basic statistical standards and procedures. If we accept the use of such sources, then we must particularly stress the need for a very conservative, objective, and skillful approach to working with them." Professor, in this paragraph, when you talk about "abnormal situations like war," what you are talking about is a complex humanitarian crisis; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I support Dr. Tabeau, because in my footnote, it says that in her report, Dr. Tabeau mentions that some sources originated from the humanitarian crisis. However, when you read the whole text, I'm saying what a demographer is duty-bound to do when using such sources, and I give the example of the Red Cross. The Red Cross is an organisation that I don't want did contest or deny. It's a humanitarian organisation which collected data on missing persons, but it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is not --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not finished. I have not finished, Madam. I have not finished. Allow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... and you can answer the question, and that was not my question. So the question now is to move down to the third paragraph, right about in the middle, where you wrote: "This does not mean that these sources cannot, at least partially, be processed by statistical specialists and sorted to ensure that they are objectively usable to the greatest possible extent." Professor, so would you agree that it is possible to use such sources, and these are these sources that you referred to in paragraph 2, that don't typically satisfy, where you wrote, "basic statistical standards and procedure"? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if, as a demographer and statistician, you do it professionally. If you adapt them in order to be able to obtain reliable data, if you're dealing with new methodologies, if you don't show how and to what extent you arrange that source, then I can't accept that. There's no source of data that a good expert, a demographer or statistician, cannot use and deal with it. It's a notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We will talk about methodology, but right now let's again just focus on sources. I'm going to ask that you turn to P10730. It's in the second binder in front of you. You have the first binder, so, yeah, it's in the second one.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just saying that my first binder is falling apart. Can I ask somebody's assistance to help me; otherwise, I'm going to lose all the pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. So you're in the second binder, P10730. Professor, are you familiar with the Iraq Body Count?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if we look at the very first page, it says: "The Iraq Body Count records the violent civilian deaths that have resulted from the 2003 military intervention in Iraq. Its public database includes deaths caused by US-led coalition forces and paramilitary or criminal attacks by others. "The Iraq Body Count's documentary evidence is drawn from cross-checked media sources of violent events leading to the death of civilians, or of bodies being found, and is supplemented by the careful review and integration of hospitals, morgues, NGOs, and official figures." Professor, you have indicated that you are not familiar with this, but I would like to turn to what would be the third --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just based on what was read, unless there's some linkage between the manner in which this body count was taken, which is very controversial -- if you ask the Bush administration, they have a very low body count. If you ask others, there is a very large body count. I'm talking about the Iraqis, not the Americans. The Americans, well, Bush is quite capable of counting American deaths. But when it comes to the Iraqis, that's another story. But when you look at how it was compiled, there is no linkage between this methodology and the one that was used in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time and particularly in Mostar; and, therefore, I think, to use this document to piggyback a question, to somehow boot-strap it in order to give validation to Ewa Tabeau's methodology is totally improper. There has to be a foundation, and one has not been led by Ewa Tabeau herself. These are incompatible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I think you can trust that the Judges will appreciate all the various facts presented before them. Madam West, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, as I said before, we're going to focus on sources right now, and not methodology. So if you go to the next part of your B/C/S, in English it's number 5 and it's entitled "Media Reports are a Vital Source of Casualty Data." If you read this --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the microphones that are not in use please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've got it, yes. What is your question, Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read this small part and then ask you a question: "Press and media reports are too rich and valuable a source to be disregarded. Media coverage of casualty information has been significantly enhanced by recent and emerging developments in technology, as has the ability to integrate this information. The IBC project exploits these developments and points to what may be possible as they evolve further." So my question, Professor, is: As you indicated in your Popovic report, would you consider media sources to be sources that could be, I quote, "processed by statistical specialists and sorted to ensure that they are objectively usable"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this goes to court and if, in court, with a minimum, those of professional and expert reliability, then the journal or magazine is not a reliability source of data that can be used as registration. But whether newspapers or television are a source of data that somebody can arrange and use, this is a very big issue. This is not just a discussion, a roundtable pannel discussion as to what happened. We are trying to arrive at a scientific conclusion in order to clarify some things. Journals, magazines, newspapers, and media stories are not a scientific source of data.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. You've indicated that they're not scientific sources, but let's go to the next page in English, at the bottom of the B/C/S, to see if it has been used by others. This is entitled "How has the Iraq Body Count work been used by others." If you go down, and you'll see it right in the B/C/S, it lists a number of categories, one being governments, inter-government agencies, lawyers, NGOs. Particularly, it lists the United States' CRS report, the United Kingdom. It goes on to list the EU, the ICC, and the WHO; and, finally, it lists the Brookings Institute and the Iraq Commission. Professor, would you concede that in some situations, and particularly in complex humanitarian crisis, like we're talking about right now, it is the norm to use unusual sources?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I can't follow you because I don't see the Brookings Institute anywhere. I can see media, governments, inter-governmental organisations, and so on and so forth. It's very difficult for me to follow you. You're reading one thing, I'm receiving a different translation, and in terms of what it's written, it's a third thing. In the meantime, I've forgotten your question. I apologise. Could you please repeat it? I really apologise. I've forgotten your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Popovic report, in which you said there were situations where you could use unusual sources, and my question was: Do you now concede, after looking at this Iraq Body Count information and people and organisations who used it, that at least in this, the Iraq situation, that might be, too, exactly what you were talking about in Popovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. You are asking me something that does not correspond to what I said in the Popovic case; not that I said it, I wrote it. What I am saying is that there are situations when you can use sources of data that were created in a humanitarian crisis, and I also quote what sources of data Dr. Tabeau lists as her sources of data that were compiled in humanitarian crises, and she also refers to certain authors. Dr. Tabeau -- this applies also to Srebrenica, and I'm also talking about the Red Cross, and about how these sources should be used, if they are used, then how a statistician can adapt them. This primarily concerned the International Organisation of the Red Cross. In this report that we are discussing at the moment and which refers to Herceg-Bosna, Dr. Tabeau uses the census which is not a humanitarian organisation source. I want to finish, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She uses a census list -- yes, I'm answering. You're asking me as if I were the one who wrote about how one should use sources that originated from humanitarian crises. I accept that Dr. Tabeau is right and that you can use them; but as a demographer, you have a duty to arrange them. In this report, there are no humanitarian data sources. The books of the war hospital might be implied as being humanitarian data sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday I did not know what the Prosecutor's questions were going to be, and I asked you what the best ideal situation would be for Ms. Tabeau to provide figures, and for independence, figures that would be certain. I had mentioned some files that she could have looked into, which she failed to do, obviously. Now we discover that there was an organisation that counted bodies in Iraq since 2003; and just to inform you, there were 30 dead in Iraq, of whom 23 in Baghdad. So the said organisation cross-checked based on media reports, hospital reports, mortuaries, NGOs, and other figures. Now, as to this cross-checking technique, is it not a technique that a demographer is bound to use before he or she reaches any safe and irrefutable conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One should check, one should compare everything. It's not just a technique, but a duty. If you're choosing, and when you're choosing your source of data, as a demographer, you have to look at all its advantages and disadvantages. You have to verify everything. You have to arrange it so as to -- for the document to give you the guarantee of a minimum reliability of the data that you will -- you're going to obtain from that source.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, we're just going to continue talking about sources. So, in this report, the OTP used the OSCE voter registry and the 1991 census as sources. Is it your testimony that the OSCE voters registry was unreliable?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you don't have to look through your report, but you can just tell me. I've gone through your report, and one of your concerns is that the OSCE doesn't have the father's name listed; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not concerned about that. I'm a demographer. I know what method Dr. Ewa Tabeau used to prove, based on the electoral rolls, that these people exist in the census and take over their ethnic structure. So this is not my --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I understand. And if you could just listen to my questions and provide the responsive answer, that will be helpful. So, again, we're talking about sources. We're not talking about methodology. So let's keep it to sources. You have mentioned many times in your report, but more clearly yesterday you said several times, that nowhere in the world, in expert and scientific research, are voters' registrations taken in this type of analysis. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that. I didn't say that. I said that I'm not aware of any scientific or professional circles ever having used electoral rolls, especially if you want to base your national structure on the data that these electoral rolls do not contain.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then, to be more exact, let me go to your report. On page 15 of your report, and this is page 14 in the B/C/S. You wrote: "Nowhere in the world, in expert and scientific research, are voters' registers taken as a starting point to make an assessment of the number of refugees." That's what you wrote; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to consult what I have written, because you have taken one sentence out of the context, after all. Give me the page, please, and which report are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your report.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first or the second?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The report entitled "A Critical Analysis of OTP Expert Reports," and then the introductory page is entitled "A Critical Analysis of OTP Expert Report, Ethnic Composition, IDPs, and Refugees." It's page 14 of that report.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the title of the report. Now, which page were you quoting from?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 14 of the B/C/S, page 15 of the English for everyone else.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 14 in B/C/S, I can't see this. Please assist me. The page starts with --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance, we can just give her a copy of the report in case she's lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you see the middle of that page, page 14?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my copy, it's page 13, and I apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see in the middle where you've bolded it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I may just take my copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, can you read the sentence in B/C/S that begins with the word "Nowhere"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm lost again. I can't find it. Are you referring to the part which starts with: "The methodological confusion ..."? I really -- I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read from your copy? I really can't find it in mine. Can somebody assist me, because what is marked in red is not the same thing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if you can read out that bolded sentence.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "It is unacceptable for economic migrants to be proclaimed refugees, and it is also impermissible to make an assessment of refugees to be done on the basis of voters' registers. Nowhere in the world, in expert and scientific research, are voters' registers taken as a starting point to make an assessment of the number of refugees."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, would this be a good place to stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott is with us. Good afternoon. We hadn't seen you in a long time. Glad to see you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, when we stopped for the break, we were talking about sources, and you had read a portion of your report in which you wrote: "Nowhere in the world, in expert and scientific research, are voters' registers taken as a starting point to make an assessment of the number of refugees." So, Professor, still talking about sources, please go to P10731. It's in the second binder. That's P10731, and the B/C/S is tab 3. This is an article from Population Studies, and it's about counting the dead in Cambodia during the Khmer Rouge regime from 1975 through 1979. I'm just going to read you the abstract and then ask you a question. Under "Abstract," it says: "Estimates of mortality in Cambodia during the Khmer Rouge regime, 1975 to 1979, range from 20.000 deaths according to former Khmer Rouge sources, to over three million victims according to Vietnamese government sources. This paper uses an unusual data source, the 1992 electoral lists registered by the United Nations, to estimate the population size after the Khmer Rouge regime and the extent of excess mortality in the 1970s. These data also provide first a breakdown of population by single year of age which allows analysis of the age structure and excess mortality and inference of the relative importance of violence as a cause of death in that period. The estimates derived here are more comparable with the higher estimates made in the past. "In addition, the analysis of likely causes of death that could have generated the age pattern of excess mortality clearly shows a larger contribution of direct or violent mortality than has been previously recognised." Professor, would you agree, and I'm asking this based on only what I've just read, just the abstract - I understand you've not read the article - but would you agree that the source used here, electoral lists, in this respect might also provide a good source for population analysis?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not read the full paper. Secondly, I don't know who wrote it. I don't know what the qualifications are of the person who wrote it, whether it's a journalist or a demographer. Secondly, you are here comparing mortality to the electoral lists. I repeat, once again, that I've never heard of electoral lists being used in scientific reports as a starting point for the estimate of the number of refugees. I underline "refugees." Really, if I had the whole paper here in front of me and if I could see what the value was of the electoral list, if I could see what is the mortality base, what data they are comparing, then I could give you my judgement. As it stands, I can either accept it or not accept it. It is a fact that this was the way in which it was done. But as to the degree of reliability of the data obtained in this way, I cannot give you my judgement. I repeat that I am not aware of anyone ever doing the estimate of the number of refugees on the basis of electoral lists or rolls.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This article is from a journal called "Population Studies" out of Great Britain. Have you ever heard of it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about several journals by that name, but I would like to hear who the author is. Perhaps I know the author, because there are -- sociologists can write about a phenomenon, a historian can write about the phenomenon. In science, everybody has the right to decide on the data sources, to select data sources. But when it's demography, then I can tell, as a demographer, what is acceptable and what is not acceptable as a minimum of reliability, minimal degree of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The author's name is Patrick Heuveline; and at the time that he wrote this, he was a demographer with the Population Studies Centre at the University of Pennsylvania, but he's currently with the University of Chicago. Have you ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue to talk about the issue of electoral records or OSCE records being used as a source. Now, you testified here at the Tribunal in June 2004 in the Blagojevic case. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was a case that involved the events of Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, for example, let's just go directly to, excuse me, your testimony, and that's going to be at page 10.990. And on that occasion, you had been asked by Mr. Karnavas whether, in the circumstances of Srebrenica, what would be the ideal source, and here you testified that the ideal source would be doing a census. And the next question was, well, in the event that you couldn't do a census, then what would you do. So the question was: "Well, let's assume that a census was not a choice for whatever reason; they had no money, they weren't interested, they couldn't carry it out, there was no political will. Whatever the situation was, what would be the next approach ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Moving on to the next page, page 10.991, your answer was: "First of all, you have to tap all the information sources that you have available. Among existing sources of information, you can make particularly good use of OSCE voter registers. We used the 1997-1998 here, but there are those that were compiled in 2000. And you can also use, as a basis or even as a guideline, the census of 1991." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're reading from the transcript, then probably that's what I said, but you can use -- you can apply that in particular for Srebrenica. I didn't think and I still don't think that this is a data source that was created in the conditions of a humanitarian crisis, but I do not consider it to be a good data source; however, you can use it. But the sense of it was that an effort to establish the number of survivors was conducted by the Prosecution expert by using only the 1997 voters' list, and at that time we also had the 2000 voters' list. The purpose or the goal was to check whether a person that is listed as missing registered to vote, and the expert was able to ascertain that nine of them were registered to vote. It is in this context that I say the method is not good. But I felt that it would be good to use not only the 1997-1998 voters' list but also the 2000 voters' list. So I'm not saying that the voters' list are ideal for the situation, but that it would have been better had the other one been used. Given that he used the 1997-1998 one, why didn't he also check the 2001, since it also existed?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your concern here is not that OSCE voters' lists are unreliable; you just thought they should use a different one?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam. These are completely different things. In that situation, you are checking whether somebody is alive. The data are not reliable, but you are trying to use the matching method to find the survivors. So you are not trying to calculate on the basis of the voters' list whether somebody became a refugee or a displaced person. You are trying to see whether, in such a limited voters' list, you're able to find any survivors. So these are different approaches used for different purposes. The voters' lists are used for different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in that case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would want to make one comment. I would appreciate if she's not interrupted. Either the questions should be narrower -- but if she's trying to extract somebody from a previous case, then the witness should be allowed to put it into perspective, because the Trial Chamber may not be aware of the facts in Srebrenica. So I would appreciate the witness being given some latitude in providing the context. Or the questions be narrower.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, in the context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, yes, per se the Trial Chamber is not supposed to be aware of the facts in the three cases in which this witness testified to search for the truth. So, please, in your preliminary question, do recall the context.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Professor, in the case of Blagojevic, that was about Srebrenica, and that was a search for the missing or the dead. So in that case, if you had used what you suggested in your testimony, the census and the voters' registration, what you would have done was compared names on the census with the names on the voters' registration. The assumption is if somebody did not register in 1997, or later as you said would be better, then they were either missing or dead. Now, that's the Srebrenica case. In our case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, that's not what she said. That's not what she said. That's not what the report says. You can mischaracterise the facts all you want. That is not what her testimony was or what she wrote as far as Blagojevic, and I should know because I tried the case and this was my witness. So either quote from the report or quote the entire passage from the record. Let's be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you were able to access the Blagojevic transcript. It would be easier to tell the witness, "In answering Mr. Karnavas' question on page this and this, this is what you said. Now, what do you add or what do you take out?" You have to make an exact reference to the Blagojevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did make an exact reference to the Blagojevic transcript, but I think we can move on to our case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, in our case, if you were applying the 1991 census and the OSCE records, the analysis would be to find out who registered in the census -- rather, who was recorded in the census, to who registered in 1997, the idea being you would see if that person was still in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, in this case, we've taken the extra step, haven't we? It's that we're looking at their address?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear that an address was sought. But before I answer this question, which is a "what if" question, I would like to tell you that in the Blagojevic report, I devote a whole chapter to the critique of the electoral rolls or voters' lists as a data source. And if I were to answer the question, "If you didn't have anything, what would you have used in addition to the 1997-1998 list," now if you ask me if I were a Prosecution expert, if I would have used the voters' list as a data source and census, as Ewa Tabeau did, then my answer would be "no," for a simple reason; or if I would have used them, my report would have contained a very specific designation as to what data were acceptable and what were not. The matching methodology applied to two incongruent data sources is something that I do not consider as guaranteeing that reliable data sources would be obtained in such a matching process. But I stress, once again, a demographer has the right to select data sources, to edit them, and to apply all scientifically approved methods and stages of work or steps, and to distance themselves and to say these data sources are dubious, but I do not have any other data sources. I can obtain this and that with a certain degree of reliability. I'm sorry, I'm not finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important here -- it is very important here, from my point of view --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The question was: Is that what we're looking at, at their address? Then your answer was not responsive. So, again, I would ask you to listen to my question and try to respond with a responsive answer. We're now talking about methodology, so I would like to go to your report to see what you've written about the issue of methodology. Now, this is page 22 of the English and page 20 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand you. I didn't understand you when you say -- I really didn't understand you. I have to understand you in order to be able to answer your questions. When you say, did we look for the address, are you saying the Prosecution, in the matching process, look for the address? Is that what mean? I don't know what you're question. What is it that you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, we're going to go on to page 20 in B/C/S of your report, and I'm going to read what you wrote in regard to matching. There you wrote: "The matching method means identifying or matching absolutely corresponding units from different sources of data; in this case, the census and voters' registers. Comparison is carried out in a way that a single identification key is first identified, according to which data from one source are let into the other source to find their identical counterparts. The matching method is not a problem if there is an exact and single identification key. The identification key consists of a number of elements of digits and letters, and the level of correctness of matching depends on correctness of each of these elements. "For example, personal identification number is a good key for matching, provided it is correct. It contains 13 digits, and each of them is an element necessary for a precise identification of a person. Its advantage is that it is unique, which means that two or more persons cannot have the same identification number, and, therefore, duplication in matching is impossible. Matching with the correct personal identification number eliminates any subjective influence on end results." So, Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, please slow down, because the interpreters find it hard to follow you. You are a very fast speaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, my question is whether, in your view of matching, would a match of the personal identification number be the ideal matching method?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best, most reliable method; not ideal, but provided that the personal ID number is unique and correct. It is unique, as the very name suggests, but it also needs to be correct. It is the most reliable key for matching. In this case, I said when you're using a cash card, you have again a numerical key, but of a different kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Had OTP used the personal identification key only, and that was the only method they used, would you disagree with the results, if it was based on that and just that entirely?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The matching method, now we have a problem with the key. If the personal ID number had been used as the key and if they had reliable and correct numbers, then the data would definitely be much more reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you go on to write, and this is at page 21 of the B/C/S, that the identification key has to be unchangeable through the matching process. Is this a view that is shared by others in the field of statistics?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not a matter of opinion. There are whole services, procedures, that are done in this manner. The census, the form is matched with the household using certain codes that are again the same for the form and for the household, and that is how you know how many members per household. The population in the countries where there are population registers, they do all those matching exercises using the personal numbers. There are states and institutions that have an established operational system for the matching process or procedure. I now cannot tell you whether there are any errors there or not, but this is the most reliable way to do it. You have to have in place an established operational system.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look to some of those states and institution. If you can go to P10734, that's in the second binder.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: P10 ... [In English] 734, yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is an article published by the US Bureau of Census, and it's entitled "Quality of Very Large Database." If you go to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the use of this document as well. This has nothing to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina. It certainly has nothing to do with her previous line of questioning, which had to do with the personal identification number, the 13 digits, and why those numbers should be unchangeable. It's not up to somebody to change those numbers. Those are given to individuals, they're unique, so what does this document have to do and what does the United States Statistical Bureau have to do with what's happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina? So I do object, unless lay a foundation as to the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the Chamber overrules. Ms. West has not even indicated what she wants to do with the document. It's premature to object.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, we were talking about methodology, and you were indicating that, in your view, a methodology that would use this personal identification number that would be unchangeable was, as you said, the best and most reliable way to do it. This is an article from the US Census Bureau, and I'm just going to read the abstract part of it and ask you a question. The abstract is: "Analysis and data-mining of large computer files are affected by the quality of the information in the files. For large population registers and for files that are ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters don't have the text in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I believe it's on the screen now, so if we can start again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "Analysis and data-mining of large computer files are affected by the quality of the information in the files. For large population registers and for files that are created by creating two or more files, duplicate entries must be identified. Duplicate identification can depend on record-linkage software that can deal with name, address, and date of birth data containing many typographical errors. "Quantitative and qualitative data must be edited to ensure that usually contradictory or missing items are changed automatically and quickly. This paper describes computational methods and software that are suitable for groups of files where individual files contain between one million and four billion records." Professor, the 1991 census indicated that Bosnia-Herzegovina had approximately 4.4 people -- million people?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the OSCE, 1997 plus 1998 voter records, were approximately 2.5 million people; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, what I've just read out in the abstract, would you agree with me that software that could computate a linkage between very large databases is something that at least the US Census Bureau advocates?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not familiar with software at all, but America has the unique register in such a way that it merges several databases, two up to 50. So different states that are part of the USA are provided databases and then they are merged, and there must be duplicates. I can't tell you what the situation is, but the state of Serbia is doing the same thing. It is trying to set up the database, but it cannot check for duplicates because it only has that particular census. It is not able to check it, and Dr. Tabeau can check it partially. For instance, if she took the JMBGs in the census and the JMBGs in the voters' list, and if she were to merge it -- Please, allow me finish. So if she were to merge those two databases--

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... my question. My question regarded linkage between software bases and the US census. Now you're talking about the Tabeau report. If you can continue on in your B/C/S version, we can exactly read about the linkage --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, please. I'm talking about merging. It says here "Merging the ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You are in an unpleasant situation. We all know this, and you are not the first and not the last. But the rules of the game are that in cross-examination, you can be asked questions that boil down to "yes," "no," "I don't remember," "I don't know." It is understandable that often you will have a desire to explain broadly. But as the time is very limited, as everyone in this courtroom will confirm to you, we must ask you to stick as precisely as possible to the questions the Prosecutor asks of you. You have no freedom of speech, as it were, here. It may be regrettable, but that's the Rules of Procedure with which we all have to comply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to be impolite, and I cannot allow you to say something. Many witnesses have already asked this question, and the answer is always the same. Please, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, we're going to move on in this article, and it's just going to be the second page of your B/C/S. And in the English, it is at the part entitled as "Number 4," the second-to-last page, and it's "Record linkage for exceptionally large files." "Many individuals believe that identifying duplicates is one of the most difficult of the data quality issues. For a large matching situation, such as matching the main Social Security Administration's file of over 600 million records against the 2000 census file of 300 million records, this may entail the detailed comparison of 600 trillion pairs of records. Matching must be done using name, address, and date-of-birth information, because the census file does not contain the social security number. Matching is done on secure administrative-record machines having two additional sets of firewalls inside the main firewalls protecting the census bureau computers. "To match efficiently, the files are matched in a series of blocking passes. During a blocking pass, only those pairs agreeing on certain characteristics are considered. For instance, on one blocking pass, only those pairs agreeing on the first and last name may be considered. Other characteristics, such as date of birth and address, are used to determine whether a pair is a match. On another pass, only those pairs agreeing on date of birth may be considered." Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we even hear the question, unless they can establish -- the Prosecution can establish that this was the procedure used in Bosnia at the time, which it was not, trying to compare this process that the United States uses in a highly-sophisticated number, with social security numbers and what have you, versus the one that was used in 1991, they are two different things. So how can she possibly answer a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The question was not even put, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please. Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's my whole point. I am raising an objection on the grounds that this document is not relevant for the comparative purposes. We already know what she's trying to do, because we've heard the previous question, and I didn't object. But now when she's going into this, it's very clear. I don't need to hear the question.
