I know the question. I can ask the question myself. She's going to be making a comparison. What I am saying is, while this may be acceptable procedure in the United States, it doesn't mean that it's acceptable, because no foundation has been laid insofar as the 1991 process. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It may very well go to credibility. It is on methodology. We'll listen to what the Prosecutor asks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, my question is whether this, what I just read, this method, sounds familiar to you. Is this the method that the OTP used in their report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say. This is not about the matching of different sources of data. This is about merging parts of one and the same source that is called a census and how by merging parts and as a result of the merge, you can end up with duplicates, how you expunge them. That has nothing whatsoever to do with the comparison of two sources of data. This is just a technology to clean the material in order to provide the reliability of the data found in the census of the USA, and this is not the same method. This is not the method which allows me to find Svetlana Radovanovic, when I compare two different sources. This is how I understand the whole matter, as I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm just going to read the second sentence again to you, which says: "For a large matching situation, such as matching the main Social Security Administration's file of over 600 million records against the 2000 census of 300 million records, this may entail a detailed comparison." Professor, this matching article from the US census is about matching different sources, correct, and it is not an article about cleaning up materials --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, madam, you are not right. If you go back to the beginning, where it says "a short overview" for large registers, the registers of population, and for databases which originate from merging two or many databases, one has to establish the duplicates. We're talking about two or more databases from the census. When one needs to establish certain, you can then compare two or more databases which refer to the population and establish whether there are any duplicates.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, nonetheless, my question is whether the sort of process is familiar to you. I'd like you to look at P09836, and that's binder 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P09836. This is the OTP report, and you can go directly -- there's a red tab, the red tab. It would be page 108 of the B/C/S, and I think you're there. I'm just going to read this paragraph and ask you a question. It's entitled "Data-Linking." It's page 94 of the English, second paragraph: "To link our data sets, we employed a multi-step procedure. Each step consisted of several comparisons between two sets of related individual-level data records. One record always describes one individual and is a collection of his or her characteristics on a number of items, such as, for example, the first name, family name ..." --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I've lost you. You're reading from page 108, the first paragraph on that page, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Second, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we'll start again: "To link our data sets, we employed a multi-step procedure. Each step consisted of several comparisons between two sets of related individual-level data records. One record always describes one individual and is a collection of his or her characteristics on a number of items, such as, for example, the first name, family name, father's name, date of birth, et cetera. All steps follow the same logic (see below). "The differences between the steps were the slightly differing criteria used to match the records, and the fact that the population available for next possible matches shrank after each step. In other words, once a number of records has been matched in two related data sets, these records were excluded from the next round of matching. In the next step, the matching criterion applied was modified compared with the previous ones to capture new matches." So, Professor, my question is: This method that the OTP report describes right here, isn't that exactly what the US census talked about, not in the abstract but in the part entitled "Record Linkage"?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the same. The USA established a link among different parts of one database; and, here, different sources are used. Different databases are used in order to establish a link surrounding one person; and, thus, you form a third database. In the USA census, nobody attempts to form a third, a seventh or a tenth database. One and only database is established, but it consists of several elements, and it has to be made reliable by discarding all duplicates. This process here consists of two databases; and by matching a third base, a database is formed through a number of steps. The first step is, I have got a match, so I will put that aside. Then I change my criteria, I modify, I match, and I add to the first match. These are the statistics of matching, as I called it. If the OTP expert said what she did and how much she matched according to the first criteria, and, for example, it would be 20 per cent, and then in the second step, the match result would be 40 per cent, according to a different set of criteria, then it would be okay. But she didn't, and that's where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But, nonetheless, Professor, would you agree that the US Census Bureau advocates a method that is very different than the single, unchangeable identification key method that you suggest?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are confusing terms. Either I'm not able to explain things properly, or I'm receiving a bad interpretation, or there is something else at stake. The USA established one database consisting of several elements. They establish it by establishing duplicates, making circles, trying to establish a database which will contain reliable data on every single person without any duplicates whatsoever. Your expert did not do the same. Your expert combines two databases into a third database. If your expert had done the following and said, "I took the census in order to establish a reliable database which will contain the exact ID numbers," it would be okay. That would be the first step. The second step, "From such census, I would like to take out those with only partial ID numbers." The third step would be identifying those with erroneous ID numbers. There is a modality that may be applied to do that. The fourth step would be to identify those without any ID numbers at all. If she had come up with an operational system of her own in order to reduce that database to one single key, that would be comparable. This is what the United States of America do, and this is what your expert should have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a problem of understanding. Perhaps I'm completely wrong. You keep stressing that the United States is using one database, the same always. I read that in the report, where we had been where, there is, on the one hand, the main Social Security Administration file and, on the other hand, the census. Now, according to you, is that the same or is that also two different bases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on which they established just one, and then what can happen to them is that both in the Social Security Administration file and in the census, they find one person. That's how I understand things when I'm reading this page. This means that I have to establish one single database which will exclude any possible duplication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, let me leave the United States and let me come back to the former Yugoslavia. The JMBG system, which seems or which is, rather, the outcome of a piece of legislation which was passed at the time in 1976, unless I'm mistaken, is a system which includes 13 entries; the date of birth, the place of birth, the gender, and one last key, which is the "K" key, which is established after a very complicated calculation. Now, when I look at this Yugoslav system, it seems to me, and again maybe I'm mistaken, that it had not provided for the ethnic background or ethnic identification as part of the 13 different entries. The fact of being a Serb, a Muslim, or a Croat was not being considered? All right. So for Mostar, for instance, the identifier, which is figure 15, because it's a city which was given a number, and for Mostar, if you're interested, that's number 15, now, if a demographer sees that a person is born in Mostar, number 15, in light of the ethnic makeup of Mostar, you know you may be wrong every one time out of two, and you say that this person is either a Muslim or a Croat. So the JMBG system is imperfect, from an ethnic point of view, because there's no reference to the ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. That explains, then, that you need to cross-reference, if I understand things correctly, with another source, which is, as is the thesis of the Prosecution, the voters' list. And in the voters' lists or roll, the ethnic background may be included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The OTP knows only too well that electoral rolls do not contain ethnic background, and they know that this is contained in the census. They need this matching exercise in order to take over the ethnicity and install it into the electoral rolls to establish a new database and proclaim it a new database which reflects the situation as it was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. If I understand you well, for a demographer or a statistician, somebody who's studied statistics, the only basis in this area is only the outcome of the census in which the citizen may or may not have indicated whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims, because they were free. That was really the only instrument available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. But you have to bear in mind that this ethnic declaration was valid at that very point in time and only at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, then. You do confirm, then, that the only reliable basis is the census, but that's not even so sure, because for the rest there is no ethnic reference at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Well, I think that's it, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to move on to a new topic. Shall I go ahead or do you want to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have two minutes and 48 seconds left. Maybe it's better to leave it at that for today, all the more, so that in 30 minutes from now, I have another trial to attend to. So we're going to continue tomorrow. Madam West, we're going to calculate the time that you've used today, and it is quite likely that we shall finish tomorrow, including with the additional questions. You've used up one hour and fifteen minutes, so you have one hour and forty-five minutes left. All right? So, Madam Witness, again these are my instructions: You shall have no contacts, neither with Mr. Karnavas, nor with the Prosecution, nor with the Judges, obviously, and we'll have the pleasure of meeting you again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of November, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
